cards.front: Protracted bacterial bronchitis: chronic wet cough; treat with a [___]-week course of amoxicillin-clavulanate; recurrent → bronchiectasis workup.
cards.context:
PBB is the most common cause of chronic wet cough in otherwise well children. Caused by persistent bacterial infection (H. influenzae, S. pneumoniae, M. catarrhalis) in airways.

Diagnosis: chronic wet cough over 4 weeks + no other features + responds to 2-4 week course of amoxicillin-clavulanate.

Recurrent or refractory PBB → workup for bronchiectasis (HRCT chest), CF, immunodeficiency.

cards.front: When acute otitis media meets criteria for antimicrobial treatment, the usual first-line oral drug is [___].
cards.context: Many cases can be observed. When age, severity, bilateral disease, perforation, or follow-up risk makes antibiotics appropriate, amoxicillin is the usual first-line choice.

cards.front: The white-cell differential is normally lymphocyte-predominant from about [___] of age until about 4-5 years, when the adult neutrophil-predominant pattern returns.
cards.context:
There are two crossovers in the white-cell differential, and both are silent traps on a report.

Neutrophils predominate at birth, hand over to lymphocytes at around one week, and take back over at about four to five years — after which the adult pattern holds for life.

So a report reading 'relative lymphocytosis' in a well toddler is describing normal physiology, and a lymphocyte-predominant film in a twelve-year-old is not.

cards.front: A flat, painless, sharply-demarcated patch of blood over the white of the eye with normal vision is a [___] haemorrhage.
cards.context:
Subconjunctival haemorrhage is benign and clears in 1-2 weeks.

In a child consider a Valsalva trigger such as coughing or vomiting (e.g. pertussis); recurrent or bilateral bleeds may flag a bleeding tendency or non-accidental injury.

cards.front: In roughly [___] per cent of cases of tetralogy of Fallot the aortic arch is right-sided, indenting the right side of the trachea.
cards.context:
The associated arch anomaly is asked because it is visible on the film.

In about a quarter of cases the aortic arch is right-sided, seen as an opacity at the upper right superior mediastinum indenting the right side of the trachea.

cards.front: In ALL, the favourable translocation is t(12;21) [___], while the poor-risk t(9;22) is the Philadelphia chromosome.
cards.context:
Two translocations carry the prognosis in paediatric ALL. t(12;21) ETV6-RUNX1 is the classic GOOD-risk marker — common and chemo-sensitive. t(9;22) — the Philadelphia chromosome, BCR-ABL1.

CNS disease (leukaemic blasts in the CSF) is also adverse.

cards.front: Using the hourly 4–2–1 rule, full maintenance for a well 15-kg child is [___] mL/hour.
cards.context: The first ten kilograms need 40 mL/hour and the next five need ten more. Illness can require a lower prescribed rate.

cards.front: CFTR modulators: ivacaftor (potentiator), lumacaftor (corrector), [___] (triple therapy covering ~90% with at least one F508del allele).
cards.context:
CFTR modulators target the protein defect, not just symptoms. Potentiators (ivacaftor) increase channel opening time.

Correctors (lumacaftor, tezacaftor, elexacaftor) help misfolded protein reach the cell surface.

cards.front: When taking a fluid history in an unwell infant, intake below [___] of the usual feed volume counts as significant reduced intake.
cards.context:
An infant turns over a far larger share of body water each day than an adult, so a feed shortfall dehydrates within hours rather than days.

Ask concretely: how many mL per feed and how many feeds today, compared with a normal day. A parent's 'feeding a bit less' often hides a major shortfall.

cards.front: Mandatory-reporting duties are jurisdiction-specific; a clinician covered by the local law reports when its threshold of [___] suspicion or belief is met, rather than waiting for proof.
cards.context:
Mandatory-reporting law differs across Australian states and territories: who must report, which maltreatment or harm is reportable, the statutory threshold and the receiving agency all vary.

Apply the law and policy for the relevant jurisdiction. The operative threshold may be reasonable suspicion or reasonable belief and may apply only to specified harm types; proof is not required before acting.

Document exact quotes, injury patterns and caregiver responses. Do not investigate or confront the suspected perpetrator — follow the local child-protection and police pathway.

cards.front: A febrile child's film shows right-sided consolidation that obliterates the right heart border while the right hemidiaphragm stays sharp. The lobe involved is the right middle lobe, because the preserved diaphragmatic outline excludes the [___] lobe.
cards.context:
This is the silhouette sign used forwards rather than recognised backwards, which is what a viva asks for. A border is visible only because aerated lung abuts it.

 The right heart border sits against the right middle lobe, so losing that border localises the consolidation to the middle lobe.

The right hemidiaphragm sits against the lower lobe — a preserved diaphragm with a lost heart border therefore excludes lower-lobe disease, without needing a lateral film.

cards.front: After nebulised adrenaline for croup, observe for symptom [___] for at least 3-4 hours; pair with dexamethasone for sustained effect.
cards.context:
Nebulised adrenaline (0.5 mL/kg of 1:1000, max 5 mL) provides rapid but TEMPORARY relief in moderate-severe croup — onset 10-30 min, duration 1-2 h.

Observe ≥3-4 h after nebulised adrenaline for symptom rebound — discharging too soon risks return in respiratory distress.

cards.front: Pyloric stenosis classically causes a hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic [___] from vomiting gastric acid.
cards.context: The biochemistry follows from vomiting pure gastric acid (HCl): lose H+ and Cl-, the kidney holds Na+ at the expense of K+ and H+, giving the classic picture. Correct fluids/electrolytes before surgery.

cards.front: A salt-wasting neonate with hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, and androgen excess most likely has [___]-hydroxylase deficiency.
cards.context:
The common 21-hydroxylase block impairs cortisol and aldosterone synthesis and diverts precursors toward androgens.

The salt-wasting form can present in the first weeks with vomiting, dehydration, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, and shock.

cards.front: Short stature = height <3rd centile for age and gender; commonest causes are [___] delay and familial short stature.
cards.context:
Short stature = height <3rd percentile for age and gender.

Pathological causes (GH deficiency, hypothyroidism, coeliac, chronic illness, Turner syndrome) are less common but require workup if growth velocity is poor.

cards.front: The classic triad of infectious mononucleosis is [___], pharyngitis, and lymphadenopathy.
cards.context:
The classic triad probes joint involvement of fever, the oropharynx (exudative pharyngitis), and lymphoid tissue (cervical lymphadenopathy, often with splenomegaly).

Bilateral posterior cervical lymphadenopathy is more specific for EBV than anterior cervical adenopathy alone — the latter is just as common in bacterial pharyngitis.

cards.front: Fever plus a hot, non-weight-bearing joint in a child is [___] arthritis until proven otherwise — aspirate urgently.
cards.context:
The can't-miss diagnosis. A hot, swollen joint with fever and refusal to bear weight is septic arthritis until proven otherwise.

It destroys cartilage within hours, so it's an emergency aspiration/washout, not a watch-and-wait.

cards.front: Modern paediatric airway measurements place the narrowest transverse dimension at the [___] opening rather than the cricoid ring; large occiput flexes the head when supine — counter with a shoulder roll.
cards.context:
Direct airway imaging and bronchoscopy show that the paediatric larynx is closer to cylindrical than the traditional funnel model; in measured transverse dimensions, the glottic opening is narrower than the cricoid ring.

Properly sized cuffed ETTs are acceptable when cuff pressure is monitored.

Large tongue + large occiput position the head in flexion when supine; place a small shoulder roll to neutralise the airway for intubation, not the head extension you'd use in an adult.

cards.front: After a toddler bites an electrical cord, the classic delayed complication is haemorrhage from the [___] artery.
cards.context:
The burn itself looks unimpressive, which is the trap — the danger is delayed, not immediate.

Bleeding typically occurs around 5-14 days later when the eschar separates. Parents must be told to expect it and how to apply direct pressure.

cards.front: An absent or asymmetric red reflex in a child needs urgent referral to exclude [___].
cards.context: A white, absent, or asymmetric red reflex is leukocoria and needs urgent ophthalmology assessment. Retinoblastoma is the life-threatening diagnosis to exclude.

cards.front: After nebulised adrenaline for croup, observe for symptom rebound for at least [___] hours; pair with dexamethasone for sustained effect.
cards.context:
Nebulised adrenaline (0.5 mL/kg of 1:1000, max 5 mL) provides rapid but TEMPORARY relief in moderate-severe croup — onset 10-30 min, duration 1-2 h.

Observe ≥3-4 h after nebulised adrenaline for symptom rebound — discharging too soon risks return in respiratory distress.

cards.front: A paediatric endotracheal tube advanced past the carina causes [___] intubation and may collapse the contralateral lung.
cards.context:
A tube advanced past the carina can enter either main bronchus and leave the contralateral lung unventilated.

The safe teaching point is the depth error: confirm the tip above the carina, bilateral air entry and bilateral aeration rather than relying on laterality.

cards.front: In Australian paediatric practice (eTG, primary-school age), symptoms recurring at least every [___] make asthma frequent rather than infrequent intermittent.
cards.context:
eTG classifies paediatric asthma by symptom PATTERN, and one interval is the discriminator that decides whether a preventer is considered at all.

Infrequent intermittent asthma needs a reliever only. Frequent intermittent asthma is a prompt to consider a daily preventer, even with normal function between episodes.

cards.front: CFTR modulators: ivacaftor (potentiator), lumacaftor (corrector), Trikafta (triple therapy covering ~90% with at least one [___] allele).
cards.context:
CFTR modulators target the protein defect, not just symptoms. Potentiators (ivacaftor) increase channel opening time.

Correctors (lumacaftor, tezacaftor, elexacaftor) help misfolded protein reach the cell surface.

cards.front: Challenge-proven IgE-mediated food allergy affects approximately [___] Australian infants at 12 months of age.
cards.context:
The HealthNuts population study found challenge-proven IgE-mediated food allergy in about 1 in 10 Australian infants at 12 months of age. That estimate should not be generalised to children of every age.

Peanut, raw egg and sesame were the principal challenge-proven allergies measured in the study; prevalence changes across childhood as some allergies resolve and others persist.

cards.front: Persistent asthma in a 6-11-year-old means daytime symptoms at least once per week, night-time symptoms at least [___] per month, or symptoms that restrict activity or sleep.
cards.context:
These are eTG's criteria, and any ONE of the three is enough — daytime frequency, night-time frequency, or functional impact.

Attribute the daytime number: AAH sets its preventer trigger at daytime symptoms twice per week or more, where eTG's persistent threshold is once per week.

Both share the night-time threshold of twice per month, and AAH adds any exacerbation needing systemic corticosteroids in the past 12 months.

cards.front: In anorectal malformations, [___] (supralevator) lesions have worse continence outcomes than low lesions.
cards.context:
High (supralevator) anorectal malformations have poorer continence outcomes than low lesions, so the anatomical level matters for prognosis and operative planning.

Staging follows level: high lesions need a defunctioning colostomy first, then a pull-through later; low lesions can have a single primary anoplasty.

Mislabelling a high lesion as low and attempting primary repair risks damaging the sphincter complex.

cards.front: In a newborn baby, jaundice from a raised [___] bilirubin fraction is always abnormal and needs urgent investigation, never just watched.
cards.context:
Why this matters: a raised conjugated (direct) fraction means bile isn't draining — biliary atresia until proven otherwise, and the surgical fix (Kasai) works far better the earlier it's caught, so this can't wait.

Contrast the everyday unconjugated jaundice of the first week (the liver just hasn't ramped up yet), which usually settles on its own.

That is why the single most useful test in a jaundiced baby is splitting the bilirubin into its two fractions.

cards.front: In a septic neonate with a central venous catheter, culture each lumen and strongly consider catheter [___] as source control.
cards.context:
A central line is both a pathogen clue and a removable focus. Culture peripheral blood and every line lumen, then strongly consider line removal in a septic neonate.

Antibiotics alone may fail while infected biofilm remains in place; fulminant disease warrants urgent infectious-diseases advice about broader cover.

cards.front: Platelets are one of the few paediatric indices with no age banding at all — the range is [___] x10⁹/L from the newborn onwards.
cards.context:
This is worth knowing precisely because almost nothing else on the paediatric panel behaves this way. The platelet range is the adult range from the first day of life onward.

That makes a low platelet count immediately meaningful at any age — no mental age-adjustment stands between the number and the diagnosis.

The corollary is also useful: reactive thrombocytosis above 400 in a child is a real finding, and is part of the supportive picture in Kawasaki disease.

cards.front: A harsh inspiratory sound heard loudest over a child's neck localises obstruction to the [___] airway.
cards.context: Stridor is turbulent airflow through a narrowed upper airway. An inspiratory sound points to an extrathoracic lesion; a fixed glottic or subglottic lesion can be biphasic.

cards.front: If lumbar puncture is unsafe or would delay treatment in a septic neonate, start meningitis-covering antimicrobials immediately and perform LP after [___].
cards.context:
Perform LP promptly and ideally before antibiotics when it is indicated and safe. Haemodynamic instability, impaired consciousness, focal signs or coagulopathy may make immediate LP unsafe.

If LP is contraindicated or would materially delay treatment, cover meningitis now and sample CSF after stabilisation; a delayed LP is safer than delayed antimicrobials.

cards.front: Wilms tumour most commonly arises in the [___].
cards.context: Wilms (nephroblastoma) is the common childhood renal tumour — a painless flank mass in a preschool child. Do not knead the abdomen.

cards.front: Transient tachypnoea of the newborn is delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid; more common after [___] delivery; resolves within 24-72 hours.
cards.context:
TTN is the commonest cause of respiratory distress in term/near-term infants in the first hours of life — delayed clearance of fetal lung fluid.

Clinical: tachypnoea 60-100/min, mild work of breathing, minimal O₂ need (FiO₂ <0.4). CXR shows 'wet lungs' — fluid in the horizontal fissure, perihilar streaking, hyperinflation.

Caesarean raises risk (no chest squeeze/catecholamine surge to absorb fluid). Self-limiting diagnosis of exclusion; trap is mistaking it for sepsis or RDS, so septic screen ± antibiotics until ruled out.

cards.front: Congenital hypothyroidism is the most common preventable cause of [___]; detected by raised TSH on newborn screen; start levothyroxine ideally within 2 weeks.
cards.context:
Congenital hypothyroidism is the most common preventable cause of intellectual disability — affects 1 in 3000-4000 live births. Detected on newborn bloodspot screening (elevated TSH).

Most common cause is thyroid dysgenesis (~85%) — agenesis, hypoplasia, or ectopic tissue.

Levothyroxine should start as soon as the diagnosis is confirmed, ideally within the first 2 weeks of life. Early treatment allows essentially normal cognitive development.

cards.front: Confidentiality with an adolescent should be explained [___] the consultation begins, not after a disclosure has already been made.
cards.context:
Say it before they disclose, not after.

A young person who has already told you something and then hears 'actually I have to report that' experiences it as a betrayal, and it is the single fastest way to lose an adolescent's trust.

The formula is short: everything stays between us, unless I'm worried you or someone else is at serious risk.

reference.title: Engaging with and assessing the adolescent patient

cards.front: Measles, varicella and tuberculosis require [___] precautions, with an N95/P2 respirator rather than a surgical mask.
cards.context:
Measles, varicella and TB need an N95/P2 respirator and a negative-pressure room — a surgical mask does not filter particles that stay suspended.

The classic exam trap is a febrile child with a rash placed in droplet precautions; if measles is on the differential, that is an airborne exposure for everyone in the room.

cards.front: Von Hippel-Lindau is characterised by haemangioblastomas of the retina and [___], with renal cell carcinoma as a major risk.
cards.context:
VON HIPPEL-LINDAU is the neurocutaneous syndrome with almost no cutaneous signs, which is why it is easy to leave off the list.

It is dominantly inherited and defined by haemangioblastomas of the retina and cerebellum, with renal cell carcinoma and phaeochromocytoma as the malignant risks.

It presents later than the others — typically young adulthood rather than childhood — so in paediatrics it usually surfaces as a family history requiring surveillance of an as-yet-well child.

cards.front: The narrowest non-distensible complete ring in a young child's airway is the cricoid, while modern measurements often find the smallest lumen at the [___].
cards.context:
Modern paediatric airway measurements often identify the glottic opening as the smallest measured lumen.

The cricoid is still the narrowest non-distensible complete cartilaginous ring and a clinically important fixed subglottic site, so swelling here can obstruct rapidly.

Keep the statements separate: smallest measured lumen = usually glottis; narrowest fixed complete ring = cricoid.

cards.front: Hydroxychloroquine is continued in essentially every child with lupus because it reduces the frequency of disease [___].
cards.context:
Hydroxychloroquine is not the drug that treats an acute flare; it is the drug that is never stopped.

It cuts how often the disease relapses, is protective in lupus nephritis, and is continued even while disease is quiet.

That background role is why it counts as the cornerstone rather than an add-on.

cards.front: Red cell distribution width (RDW) reports the variation in red cell [___], which is why it rises early in iron deficiency.
cards.context:
Red cell distribution width is a spread, not an average, which is why it moves before the mean cell volume does.

In early iron deficiency the marrow starts making small cells while older normal ones are still circulating, so the population becomes mixed.

Thalassaemia trait makes uniformly small cells instead, so its RDW usually stays normal.

cards.front: The white-cell differential is normally lymphocyte-predominant from about 1 week of age until about [___] years, when the adult neutrophil-predominant pattern returns.
cards.context:
There are two crossovers in the white-cell differential, and both are silent traps on a report.

Neutrophils predominate at birth, hand over to lymphocytes at around one week, and take back over at about four to five years — after which the adult pattern holds for life.

So a report reading 'relative lymphocytosis' in a well toddler is describing normal physiology, and a lymphocyte-predominant film in a twelve-year-old is not.

cards.front: Many conditions mimic seizures but are NOT epileptic; key to diagnosis is detailed [___] from witness + home video (more useful than interictal EEG).
cards.context:
Many paroxysmal conditions mimic seizures — accurate diagnosis prevents unnecessary anti-epileptic therapy.

History from witness + home video is far more useful than EEG (which is often normal between events).

cards.front: An unvaccinated 3-year-old starting MMR catch-up needs a minimum interval of [___] between the two MMR-containing doses.
cards.context:
For an unvaccinated child needing MMR catch-up, the Australian Immunisation Handbook specifies a minimum interval of 4 weeks between the two doses.

Minimum intervals depend on the vaccine, dose number, age and product. Check the Handbook tables when deciding whether an earlier dose is valid.

Return to the routine schedule once catch-up is complete. One minimum interval does not apply to every vaccine.

cards.front: A competent fifteen-year-old describes school absences after peer conflict. There is no immediate safety concern. Before contacting the school for collateral history, obtain the young person’s [___].
cards.context:
Discuss privacy and its safety limits early in the consultation. The young person should understand what information you propose to share and with whom.

Explore attendance, peer relationships and bullying directly with the adolescent; collateral information supplements their account.

reference.title: Engaging with and assessing the adolescent patient

cards.front: Pathognomonic [___] spots on buccal mucosa plus cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, and a cephalocaudal rash = measles.
cards.context:
Koplik spots are tiny grain-of-salt white papules on an erythematous buccal mucosa, appearing 1-2 days before the measles rash.

They are the feature that lets you call measles before serology returns. The public-health move is immediate isolation and notification, because measles is infectious from 4 days before to 4 days after rash onset.

cards.front: Gold-standard diagnosis of paediatric OSA is overnight polysomnography; distinguishes true OSA from [___] snoring (benign).
cards.context:
PSG measures airflow, respiratory effort, oxygenation, EEG, ECG, movement to characterise sleep-disordered breathing.

Practically: overnight sleep-lab stay is expensive with long waiting lists, so many centres treat clinically without PSG when adenotonsillar hypertrophy is obvious.

cards.front: A bronchodilator relieves the obstruction of asthma but not that of [___], where small-airway oedema, epithelial debris and mucus plugging predominate.
cards.context:
Asthmatic narrowing is mostly bronchial smooth-muscle spasm plus mucosal inflammation, so a beta-2 agonist can relax it within minutes.

In infant viral small-airway disease, oedema, epithelial debris and mucus predominate. Routine bronchodilators do not improve clinically important outcomes; non-response does not prove bronchoconstriction never occurs.

cards.front: The pictorial scale grading stool consistency from type 1 (hard lumps) to type 7 (watery) is the [___] stool chart.
cards.context:
Types 1-2 indicate constipation, 3-4 are normal, and 6-7 are loose or watery. A shared pictorial scale matters because families' words for 'normal poo' vary enormously.

In constipation review, progress is tracked as movement from types 1-2 toward 3-4, not just stool frequency.

cards.front: Slipped capital femoral epiphysis in an adolescent is treated as a [___] emergency.
cards.context: SCFE is a surgical emergency in overweight 10–14-year-olds: the epiphysis slips through the physis. Knee pain may be referred — always examine the hip.

cards.front: For a likely viral or uncomplicated self-limiting syndrome, good antibiotic stewardship may mean [___] antibiotics with safety-net review.
cards.context:
The decision not to prescribe is part of antimicrobial competence.

RCH recommends no routine antibiotics for most uncomplicated acute otitis media and notes that most infectious diarrhoea does not benefit from antibiotics.

Treat pain, hydration and safety-netting while reserving antibiotics for the syndrome's defined high-risk, severe or complicated features.

cards.front: A child falls and chips both upper incisors. The yellow surface is sensitive to air and cold, and there is no pink pulp. The exposed tissue is [___].
cards.context:
Enamel-dentine fractures expose dentinal tubules, which are sensitive to air and cold.

Dental review within 24 hours seals the surface.

cards.front: In a neonate, hypothermia or temperature instability can be a sepsis sign even without fever; normal blood pressure is not reassuring because hypotension is [___].
cards.context:
Neonates often cannot mount a localised inflammatory response. Poor feeding, apnoea, lethargy, weak cry, temperature instability or respiratory deterioration may be the whole presentation.

Hypotension is a late sign; a normal blood pressure does not exclude evolving neonatal shock.

cards.front: Fetal pulmonary vascular resistance is high (lungs are fluid-filled, not gas-exchanging). The pulmonary artery → aorta shunt is the ductus arteriosus; the right atrium → left atrium shunt is the foramen [___].
cards.context:
Fetal lungs are fluid-filled, so pulmonary vascular resistance is HIGH — higher than systemic, because the placenta is a huge low-resistance bed. Blood shunts right-to-left, away from the lungs.

Two lung bypasses: the foramen ovale, right atrium to left, taking the best-oxygenated blood to brain and coronaries; and the ductus arteriosus, pulmonary artery to aorta.

At birth the lungs inflate, resistance falls and the placenta goes, so both shut. Trap: a duct-dependent baby looks well at birth and collapses over days as the duct closes.

cards.front: SCID = severe combined immunodeficiency; presents with [___] infections + FTT; absent thymus on CXR; stem cell transplant before 3.5 months gives best outcomes.
cards.context:
Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) is the most severe primary immunodeficiency — defective T-cell development with variable B-cell involvement. Lab signature: lymphopenia (especially T cells), absent thymus on CXR.

Without treatment, infants present with opportunistic infections (PJP, CMV, fungi) and FTT in first months.

Early diagnosis and infection prevention improve transplant survival. Transplant by 3.5 months is associated with high survival; older infection-free infants can also do well.

cards.front: A positive stool reducing-substances test after gastroenteritis most commonly indicates transient [___] intolerance.
cards.context:
Rotavirus flattens villi and strips their brush-border lactase, so lactose passes to the colon unabsorbed. Unabsorbed reducing sugars in stool turn the test positive.

Sucrose is not a reducing sugar — a negative test does not exclude sucrase deficiency.

cards.front: A baby born at 29 weeks is now 16 weeks old chronologically. The corrected age for developmental interpretation is [___] weeks.
cards.context:
Corrected age equals chronological age minus the number of weeks born before 40 weeks.

A baby born at 29 weeks was 11 weeks early; at 16 weeks chronological age, developmental skills are interpreted at about five weeks corrected age.

Use corrected rather than chronological age when deciding whether a preterm infant has missed a developmental profile.

cards.front: Hand-foot-mouth disease (Coxsackie A16) may be followed by nail [___] (onychomadesis) weeks after; this is self-limiting and needs no treatment.
cards.context:
Onychomadesis (proximal nail-bed separation) follows hand-foot-mouth disease in some children weeks after the acute infection has resolved. The mechanism is temporary nail matrix arrest from systemic viral illness.

Parents often present anxiously after noticing the nails 'falling off' — reassure: self-limiting, nails regrow normally, no treatment needed.

cards.front: Bordetella pertussis is a Gram-negative aerobic coccobacillus; mortality is ~1 in [___] babies under 6 months.
cards.context:
Bordetella pertussis is a Gram-negative aerobic coccobacillus — it colonises ciliated respiratory epithelium and acts via secreted toxins (it is not an intracellular pathogen).

Azithromycin is given to eradicate the organism and limit spread, not because the bacterium hides inside cells. Infant mortality reflects apnoea and pulmonary hypertension from severe paroxysmal coughing.

Maternal vaccination in pregnancy + cocoon strategy is the main protection for infants too young for their own vaccine.

cards.front: Direct questions about suicide do [___] increase suicide risk; asking shows you take distress seriously and opens dialogue.
cards.context:
The myth that asking about suicide 'plants the idea' is wrong. Cochrane evidence confirms direct questioning does NOT increase suicide risk — it may reduce it by signalling that you take the distress seriously.

Ask in stepwise escalation: mood → 'life not worth living' → 'thought about ending your life' → plan → access to means. Document verbatim.

cards.front: Kernicterus = irreversible bilirubin encephalopathy from the unconjugated form crossing the blood-brain barrier and depositing in the basal ganglia; chronic sequelae include [___] cerebral palsy and sensorineural hearing loss.
cards.context:
Kernicterus is irreversible bilirubin encephalopathy — unconjugated bilirubin crosses the blood-brain barrier, deposits in basal ganglia, and causes neurological damage.

Chronic sequelae: choreoathetoid cerebral palsy, sensorineural hearing loss, dental enamel hypoplasia.

Risk factors lower the threshold: prematurity, sepsis, acidosis, hypoalbuminaemia (less protein binding).

cards.front: Air trapping is confirmed with paired inspiratory and [___] chest films, or with decubitus views when the child cannot cooperate.
cards.context:
Two films confirm air trapping, and the choice between them is about whether the child can cooperate.

An older child can hold inspiration and expiration for paired frontal films. A toddler cannot, so decubitus views are used instead; brief fluoroscopy is a further option.

cards.front: A 4-month-old's raised bright-red lump on the arm was not there at birth and has grown since week 3. Her parents are reassured that this [___] will shrink on its own over years.
cards.context:
Superficial lesions start proliferating at 1 to 4 weeks and reach about 80% of final size by 3 months; deep ones start later and look bluish.

Growth slows after that and plateaus by 6 to 9 months; involution is mostly complete by about 4 years. A lesion present at birth that never shrinks is usually a vascular malformation.

Site changes the plan: near the eye or ear it threatens function, around the lips or anus it ulcerates, and in a beard distribution it can hide an airway lesion.

cards.front: Most paediatric arrests are respiratory in origin (60%) or circulatory failure (30%); primary cardiac causes are rare unlike adults — so prioritise [___] over defibrillation.
cards.context:
Paediatric arrests are usually secondary to respiratory failure or circulatory collapse, not primary cardiac arrhythmia.

So the highest-yield intervention is effective ventilation, not defibrillation — the opposite priority to adult VF arrest.

cards.front: For status without IV access, RCH prefers buccal/IN [___] over rectal diazepam.
cards.context:
Rectal diazepam (Stesolid) was the historical community option, but RCH acute seizure guidance now lists midazolam first-line for non-IV routes (0.3 mg/kg buccal/IN).

Teach the preferred modern agent and route rather than memorising a legacy rectal dose that current RCH CPGs no longer table.

cards.front: The first-line antibiotic for pertussis is [___].
cards.context:
Bordetella pertussis colonises the surface of ciliated respiratory epithelium (it is not an intracellular pathogen).

Macrolides — azithromycin first-line — eradicate carriage and cut transmission; by the paroxysmal stage the cough is toxin-driven so antibiotics do little for the patient's symptoms.

cards.front: Non-blanching purpuric rash with fever is [___] until proven otherwise — treat before LP.
cards.context:
A non-blanching purpuric rash represents endothelial damage + intravascular platelet consumption — in a febrile child, this is meningococcal sepsis until cultures say otherwise.

Antibiotic before everything else: IV (or IM if no access) ceftriaxone as soon as suspected; LP, blood cultures, full work-up follow but do not delay the dose.

For children ≥2 months, RCH often uses 100 mg/kg daily while eTG uses 50 mg/kg 12-hourly (max 2 g per dose); follow local AMS. Younger infants require age-specific neonatal regimens.
